issues.legal_issue: A party may not amend a written statement to withdraw a categorical admission and thereby displace the opposing party’s case when the admission remains attributable to that party.
material_facts: The respondent first filed a written statement accepting the appellant’s case in its entirety, including his claim to a share under the will.
The respondent later sought to replace or amend that statement to deny the claim and the will.
The respondent’s challenge that she had not engaged the advocate or signed the first written statement was rejected after an inquiry found that she had engaged the advocate and filed the statement.
The proposed amendment would have repudiated the earlier admission, rather than merely explaining or clarifying it.
Other defendants’ dispute of the will did not alter the fact that the respondent sought to resile from her own admission.
issues.conclusion: The amendment allowing the respondent to resile from her categorical admission could not stand. The appeal was allowed and the impugned judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments are considered liberally but the court must exercise its discretion judiciously. A categorical admission in a pleading is a judicial admission, admissible against its maker and capable of dispensing with proof under Section 58 of the Evidence Act; admissions may also have consequences under Order VIII Rule 5 and Order XII Rule 6 of the Code. A party cannot amend a pleading to withdraw such an admission so as to displace the opposing party’s case. An admission may, where its nature permits, be explained or clarified, and alternative pleas may be taken if they are not mutually destructive. The Court relied on Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co., Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, Sangramsinh P. Gaekwad v. Shantadevi P. Gaekwad, Union of India v. Pramod Gupta, State of Haryana v. M.P. Mohla, and Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam. Heeralal treated Akshaya Restaurant v. P. Anjanappa as per incuriam to the extent it conflicted with the rule in Modi Spinning; the Court distinguished cases concerning explanation of an admission or amendments that did not erase it.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_case and categorical_admission and proposed_amendment_erases_admission and admission_authorship_challenge_rejected

predicates.written_statement_amendment_case: A party seeks to amend a written statement already filed in the proceeding.
predicates.categorical_admission: The party’s written statement unequivocally accepts the opposing party’s case on the matter in dispute.
predicates.proposed_amendment_erases_admission: The proposed amendment repudiates the admission and would displace the opposing party’s case rather than merely explain or clarify the admission.
predicates.admission_authorship_challenge_rejected: The party’s claim that the admission was not made by or attributable to that party is rejected.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to amend a written statement to erase an unequivocal admission, and the admission is found to be attributable to that party, the amendment is denied.
